title: Validating conversation keywords against attitudes, with a no-chat arm and delayed follow-up
why: Addresses design and measurement: a no-chatbot arm identifies the chatbot's contribution, a pre-chat attitude measure ties keywords to belief change, and a wave 2 tests durability.

power_target.basis: H1 MDE 0.3985 at 224/215 per arm; observed 0.638. Because the chat increment is likely smaller than the full effect, consider about 400 per arm.

rationale: In the source study both arms chatted, so the 0.64-point shift (95% CI [0.37, 0.91]) cannot be split between the op-ed and the chatbot. Keyword gaps of 16.6 and 26.7 percentage points may reflect echoing of the op-ed rather than changed belief, and attitudes were measured only once, right after exposure.
contribution: Identifies the chatbot's added effect beyond the op-ed text, checks whether keyword use tracks real attitude change, and tests whether the effect lasts.
hypothesis: If conversation adds persuasion beyond the text, the op-ed+chat arm will shift attitudes more than the op-ed-only arm, and the difference will persist at 2 weeks. If it does not, the arms will not differ, or the chat-driven difference will fade. Within the op-ed+chat arm, argument-adoption coding should predict attitude shift better than keyword counts.
primary_outcome: Immediate change in support toward the op-ed position (post minus pre), with the 2-week change as the durability outcome.
comparison: Op-ed+chatbot versus op-ed only (chatbot increment); op-ed versus placebo (text effect); wave 2 versus wave 1 change; keyword and adoption measures as predictors of shift within the op-ed+chat arm.
unresolved: Op-ed and placebo article texts, chatbot configuration and keyword dictionary must be supplied by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation, including the wave 2 bonus, must be supplied.
Wave 2 is fielded as a separate session; the flow here lists it in sequence.
label: Design advance

title: Oversampling the anti-spending position and varying topic
why: Addresses sample and power: the anti-spending group (n=59) could not test moderation (interaction p=0.37).

power_target.basis: Anti-spending effect of 0.23 (SE 0.454 at n=59); detecting 0.23 needs about 650 per cell at SD 1.49, so 250 per arm detects only about 0.35 within a subgroup. Size to the interaction as the target.

rationale: The source op-ed effect was 0.64 points overall, but only 59 participants were anti-spending (effect 0.232, SE 0.454), and the position interaction was 0.425 (p=0.37), so moderation is untested. Only one topic (spending) was used, so topic generality is unknown.
contribution: Tests whether the op-ed plus chatbot effect holds for anti-spending respondents and on a second, unrelated policy topic, using adequately powered interaction tests.
hypothesis: The op-ed moves attitudes toward the op-ed position relative to placebo in both position groups and on both topics. The treatment by position and treatment by topic interactions are small relative to the main effect.
primary_outcome: Support moved toward the op-ed position (1-7 recoded), as in the source study.
comparison: Op-ed + chatbot versus placebo + chatbot, with interactions of treatment with prior position (pro vs anti) and with topic.
unresolved: Choice of the second policy topic and the op-ed, placebo and chatbot texts for each topic and position must be written by the research team.
Topic assignment and quota logic must be implemented in the survey platform.
IRB approval and participant compensation must be supplied by the research team.
label: Generalizability

media: oped: image stimulus to supply (the op-ed article text arguing against the participant's spending position)
chat_arg: image stimulus to supply (embedded chat window with an assistant that argues the op-ed's side)
chat_neu: image stimulus to supply (embedded chat window with an assistant that asks only neutral questions)
title: Chatbot as persuader versus passive measurement
why: Addresses design and framing by discriminating between the 'adds value' and 'superficial engagement' positions of D1.

power_target.basis: Chat increment is expected to be at most about half the observed 0.64; the SD of 1.49 from the H1 row gives MDE about 0.29 at 400 per arm.

rationale: The source study gave the chatbot to both arms, so the 0.64-point shift (SD about 1.49 in H1) cannot be attributed to the chatbot rather than the op-ed. Attitudes were also measured only right after exposure. This design randomises the chatbot's role after the same op-ed and adds a 1-week follow-up.
contribution: Separates the chatbot's persuasive role from the op-ed's effect and tests whether any added shift lasts.
hypothesis: If conversation adds persuasive value (position a), the arguing chatbot arm shows more shift toward the op-ed than both other arms. If engagement is superficial (position b), the arms do not differ and any shift decays by 1 week.
primary_outcome: Support moved toward the op-ed position (1-7, recoded so higher means closer to the op-ed), immediate and at 1 week.
comparison: Arguing chatbot vs neutral chatbot vs static task on immediate and 1-week shift; the arguing vs static contrast is the main one.
unresolved: The op-ed text, the chatbot prompts and the hosting of the chat widget must be supplied by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation levels need to be supplied.
The follow-up link delivery and panel re-contact mechanism need to be arranged.
label: Theoretical debate
